title: The development and application of the emotional dimensions of a soundscape

findings.mechanism: Principal Component Analysis of semantic differential ratings reveals underlying emotional dimensions of soundscape perception.
findings.quote: Component 1 was found to explain 60% of the variance and had high positive loadings for “Calmness and Relaxation” and “Intrusiveness”, and also with "Comfort and Reassurance”.

findings.mechanism: Natural sound elements (birdsong) enhance calmness perception.
findings.quote: a park with birdsong was rated highly calming, but not so vibrant

findings.mechanism: Natural sound elements (birdsong) may not enhance vibrancy as much as other elements.
findings.quote: a park with birdsong was rated highly calming, but not so vibrant

findings.antecedent: adding 'new things' (general intervention) to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: Introduction of additional sounds alters the overall emotional perception of the soundscape.
findings.quote: adding new things into the soundscape reduced the feeling of calmness.

findings.antecedent: adding 'church bells' to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: Specific sound elements (church bells) can enhance vibrancy.
findings.quote: Church bells, rowdiness and nearby traffic were all shown to increase the feeling of vibrancy

findings.antecedent: adding 'rowdiness' to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: Specific sound elements (rowdiness) can enhance vibrancy.

findings.antecedent: adding 'air-conditioning units' to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: Specific sound elements (AC units) can decrease vibrancy.
findings.quote: air-conditioning units, birdsong and a water fountain all decreased the feeling of vibrancy.

findings.antecedent: adding 'birdsong' to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: Specific sound elements (birdsong) can decrease vibrancy (or shift perception towards calmness).

findings.antecedent: soundscapes with 'roughly the same dB(A) level' (e.g., 64-66 dBA)
findings.mechanism: Subjective emotional perception of soundscapes is not solely determined by objective acoustic measures like dB(A).
findings.quote: many of the recordings have roughly the same level, but they are perceived very differently for calmness and vibrancy.

stimuli.description: 8 different urban soundscape recordings (Experiment 1 & 2), 13 different soundscape recordings (application section) including common urban settings and modified versions with added sounds (e.g., AC units, water fountain, birds, church bell, traffic, rowdiness). Recordings were 8-second excerpts.
Images of recording locations presented with soundscapes (Experiment 2A).

tables.description: Starting set of 5 emotional dimensions and their semantic descriptors used in the semantic differential rating scales.
Component Score Coefficient Matrices (Varimax Rotation) for Experiment 1, 2A, and 2B, showing loadings of 5 semantic dimensions on two principal components and variance explained by each component.

Sample of 13 soundscape recordings used for exploring applications of the calmness-vibrancy perceptual space, including objective acoustic parameters (Intelligibility, Sound Pressure Level, Loudness, Sharpness, Roughness, Fluctuation Strength).

limitations: Demographic issues require data from large populations to understand nuances between different demographic groups.
Listening state ('tuned in' or 'tuned out') and intended user activities affect soundscape perception and need to be considered in design.
There are often considerable differences between quantitative measurements of acoustic comfort and subjective evaluation of soundscapes.
More evidence is needed to understand how different design interventions will position soundscapes within the perceptual space.
Challenges of context, personal experience, cognition, and subjectivity in assessing soundscapes make the task considerable.
